**The C-HAWQ 10-Step Proven Process — Visual Overview**

**How the Four Phases Work**
Phase 1 — Discovery (Steps 1–4) | 2–4 Weeks Fast-moving. We identify, meet, qualify, and schedule. Most of this work happens at events and on calls. AI handles research and drafts follow-up communications; the team handles face-to-face relationships.
Phase 2 — Development (Steps 5–6) | 1–2 Months We go deeper inside the municipality and build the project package. Science, engineering, and funding all come together. The Champion starts to see a real path forward.
Phase 3 — Mobilization (Steps 7–8) | 4–6 Months We bring the vision to life in the community and create the political conditions for a yes vote. This is the most relationship-intensive phase.
Phase 4 — Execution (Steps 9–10) | 1–2 Years The project becomes real. Agreements are signed, funding is secured, work begins, and the win gets documented and amplified.

title: Lead Generation Strategy & Content Engine
text:
**Lead Generation Strategy & Content Engine**

**Primary Targeted List — SFWMD Partnership**
C-HAWQ’s primary targeted list flows from the South Florida Water Management District partnership and grant program. As C-HAWQ establishes its grant program through SFWMD, municipalities within SFWMD’s district that have qualifying projects will be the primary pipeline source. This relationship is the cornerstone of C-HAWQ’s institutional outreach and is managed at the Executive level.
Secondary natural discovery channels: - Conferences and events (documented throughout this binder) - Referrals from completed projects (Step 10) - Referrals from the academic and advisor network - Organic inbound via the C-HAWQ website and grant portal
Assumption: The team does not need to proactively cold-source a long list of municipal targets. The SFWMD partnership, active conference presence, and referral network will naturally surface qualifying leads at a pace consistent with the 3-year pipeline targets in Section 2D.

**Mana Vision — Content Marketing Engine**
What it is: Mana Vision is C-HAWQ’s content generation platform — a marketing engine that publishes relevant scientific content intersected with C-HAWQ’s work across digital channels. It keeps C-HAWQ visible to Simmer contacts, supports the 1,000,000 digital impressions target in the VTO, and builds C-HAWQ’s authority as a thought leader in coastal science.
What it posts: Science-driven content relevant to Florida coastal municipalities — water quality data, habitat restoration outcomes, C-HAWQ project updates (as they develop), and intersections of policy and environmental science.
Management: Emily Begin approves content for Mana Vision initially. Management transitions to Ryan Begin or Lorine Najjar as capacity allows.
Content progression: - Early stage (now): Science education, Florida water quality trends, C-HAWQ mission content - As projects mature: Project updates, milestones, before/after imagery from Ryan Begin’s documentation - Post-completion: Case studies and use case content from Step 10 deliverables
Connection to Simmer contacts: Opted-in Simmer contacts (those with Opted-In-Mana tag in GHL) receive Mana Vision content distributions. This is the primary nurture channel for long-term relationship maintenance. See Module C for opt-in consent requirements.

**Pipeline Health Check — Monthly Format**
Run this check the first Monday of every month. Takes 20–30 minutes. Produce a one-paragraph written summary filed in the team’s shared Google Drive folder under Pipeline Reviews.
The 5 questions:
Lead volume: How many new leads were added to GHL this month? Are we on pace for the year’s target?
Qualification rate: Of leads that had a discovery meeting (Step 3), what percentage got a Go or Conditional Go? If below 25%, revisit discovery meeting quality or lead sourcing.
Phase 2 load: How many projects are currently active in Steps 5–6? Are any approaching the 8–10 cap? Do any need to be paused?
Champion temperature: For every active Phase 3 project (Steps 7–8), when was the last touchpoint with the Champion? Any going cold?
Pipeline velocity: Are projects advancing through phases at expected timelines? Anything stuck?

title: ⚠ Critical Insurance Gaps
text:
**⚠ Critical Insurance Gaps**
Gap 1 — Field work is not covered under Class 8810. The clerical office classification does not cover field activities including water sampling, boat operations, event setup/teardown, or outdoor community events. If a C-HAWQ team member is injured during field work or event operations, the current Workers’ Comp policy may not respond.
Recommended action for future projects: Contact The Hartford or your agency (Specialty Program Group, 866-467-8730) to add the appropriate field/outdoor worker class codes to the policy. Likely codes to discuss: Class 9102 (Parks and playground employees) or equivalent environmental field worker code for Florida.
Gap 2 — No General Liability policy. C-HAWQ should carry General Liability insurance to cover: - Third-party bodily injury or property damage at events - Operations on municipal property (waterways, parks, public spaces) - Booth operations at conferences (many venues require a Certificate of Insurance) - Any claims arising from the mobile science museum experience
Recommended action: Obtain a General Liability policy (minimum $1M per occurrence / $2M aggregate recommended for nonprofit environmental organizations with event activity). Request Certificates of Insurance naming municipalities as additional insured when working on their property.
Gap 3 — Graduate students and volunteers are not C-HAWQ employees. Workers’ Comp does not cover non-employees. For field work: - University-enrolled students: their university’s general liability and student insurance may provide coverage — confirm with each professor’s department - Community event volunteers: covered by a participant liability waiver (see template below)

**STEP 1: DISCOVER THE MUNICIPAL CHAMPION**

**The Why — What This Step Accomplishes**
The Municipal Champion is a decision-maker who is personally driven to improve their local coastal environment but is stalled — by funding gaps, political friction, or engineering complexity. C-HAWQ’s role is to find these people, make a first connection, and get their contact info into GHL so follow-up can happen. That’s it. This step is about discovery, not pitching.

**The Three Ways We Meet Champions**
There are three channels. The difference between them is how the conversation is captured:
The key distinction is simple: If you’re at an event, wear the Plaud Pin and it records everything. If you’re introduced over the phone or on a video call, make sure recording is on from the start.

**What to Do When You Meet Someone**
Have a natural conversation. Lead with curiosity about them and their community — not a pitch.
Get their contact info: business card, email, or phone number. Failing that, photograph their name badge (ask first) or connect on LinkedIn.
Add them to GHL the same day — Boil or Simmer tag (see GHL Reference Guide, Module C).
Give the recording or your notes to the AI agent for follow-up email drafting.

**Cold Outreach Email Templates — Step 1 Sequence**

No pitch — just want to understand what you’re working with. > > [Your Name] | C-HAWQ | chawq.org

title: STEP 2: IMPRESS & ENGAGE EMOTIONALLY
text:
**STEP 2: IMPRESS & ENGAGE EMOTIONALLY**

**The Why — What This Step Accomplishes**
The first real engagement with a prospect is not a sales pitch — it’s an experience. We create immediate emotional connection through our immersive science story. We translate rigorous coastal science into something relatable, urgent, and personal for whoever we’re talking to. The goal: they leave this interaction feeling like C-HAWQ is the team that can finally make their project real.

**The Immersive Engagement — What It Is**
The C-HAWQ immersive engagement is our mobile, multi-sensory experience. It includes:
Immersive visuals of coastal habitats before and after intervention
Real scientific data presented in human terms
Academic speakers or video testimonials
Interactive demonstrations of the impact of water quality on local ecosystems
This engagement happens most often at conferences and industry festivals where we have a booth or speaking slot, but the approach — science made emotional and real — applies in every one-on-one conversation.

**Conference/Festival Booth Protocol**
Before the Event: 1. Complete the Conference Pre-Research AI prompt (Section 3.1) 2. Confirm booth setup: displays, handouts, About Us deck loaded, demo materials ready 3. Assign roles: who is working the booth, who is floating/networking 4. Brief the team: what’s the target audience, what’s the one-liner, what are the qualifying questions
At the Event — Booth Operations: 1. Wear Plaud Pin. Record from the moment you arrive. 2. Engage everyone who stops — your opening is the science story, not a pitch 3. The opening: “Have you ever seen what a restored seagrass bed looks like? Let me show you something.” 4. For every promising contact: get their info (business card, email, name badge photo) 5. Log each meaningful conversation immediately in your notes app or on paper 6. Take photos of name badges (with permission) for follow-up processing
The One-Liner (use when someone asks what C-HAWQ does): “We help coastal Florida municipalities get their stalled water and habitat projects unstuck — we bring the science, the community engagement, and up to $200K in technical assistance to make it happen.”
Qualifying Questions at the Booth: - “What does your municipality/organization work on for water quality?” - “Are there any projects in the pipeline that haven’t been able to move forward?” - “What’s typically the biggest blocker when you try to get something like that off the ground?” - “Have you heard of the P3 model for funding environmental projects?”

**The Conference Conversation Script**
When you’re at a booth or networking session, use this five-part framework to move from introduction to a qualified next step:
PART 1 — THE HOOK (30 seconds)
Open with the science story — not who we are. Create curiosity before you create context.
“Can I show you something? This is what [local waterway name / a Florida coastal estuary] looked like thirty years ago — and this is what it looks like today. That didn’t happen by accident.”
If you don’t have visuals: “We work in coastal Florida — and the scale of what’s been lost in the last two decades in just this region alone is something most people don’t realize until they see the data.”
The hook is not a pitch. It’s a question that invites them into a conversation.
PART 2 — THE PIVOT (From “Wild Idea” framing to “Pre-Funding” framing)
Listen for the moment they acknowledge a problem. Then shift the frame from dream to possible.
Common response you’ll hear: “We’d love to do something like that but there’s no money for it.”
Your pivot: “That’s actually exactly the scenario we were built for. Most municipalities we work with aren’t waiting on a project — they’re waiting on the pathway to fund it. That’s the gap we fill.”
Then: “Are you in the early stages of something — or is this more of a ‘we know we need to do something but haven’t started yet’?”
This distinction matters. Early-stage vision is our sweet spot. We don’t compete with projects that already have engineers under contract.
PART 3 — PROBING QUESTIONS (Qualification without interrogation)
Once they’ve acknowledged a project or problem area, go deeper:
“What’s the waterbody or habitat you’re most concerned about?”
“Who inside [city/county] is really driving this — is there one person who won’t let it die?”
“Has there been any engineering work done, or is this still purely in the vision stage?”
“What do you think the biggest obstacle has been — funding, political will, or both?”
You’re listening for: a real municipal champion, an early-stage project, and a funding gap. All three = GO.
PART 4 — THE PITCH (The Catalyst Moment)
When qualification is confirmed, deliver the value proposition clearly:
“Here’s what C-HAWQ does differently: we bring up to $200,000 in Exploration Funds — fee-free technical assistance — to do the science and engineering work needed to get a project to an approvable form. We’re not an engineering firm. We’re the bridge between the vision your municipality has and the moment it becomes a real project.”
“We’ve seen cities sit on these projects for five, ten years because they couldn’t get the science right or the funding lined up. The Exploration Grant gets that work done — and it costs the municipality nothing to find out if it’s possible.”
Key phrase: “$200,000 Exploration Grant — at no cost to the municipality.” Use it. It’s the single most effective thing we say.
PART 5 — CLOSE & TIE-DOWN (Get the next step)
Never leave a conversation without a next step:
“It sounds like this is worth a real conversation. Can I get your card? I’d love to send you some information on how the Exploration Grant works and schedule a 20-minute call.”
If they’re clearly the right person: “Who would need to be on that call from your side? Sometimes it’s worth having the City Manager or Director involved from the start so we’re not playing phone tag later.”
If they’re lukewarm: “Even if the timing isn’t right now, let me get your info — projects like this have a way of coming back around, and it’s worth knowing we exist.”
After the conversation: Log the name, organization, qualification level (Boil vs. Simmer), what project they mentioned, and any next step committed. Do this before the next conversation, not at the end of the day.
After Each Day: 1. Export and name your Plaud recordings: YYYY_MM_DD_EventName_DayX_YourName 2. Run the Post-Event Plaud AI prompt (Section 3.2) 3. Add new contacts to GHL 4. Send follow-up emails that evening or first thing next morning

**Speaking Slot Protocol**
If C-HAWQ has a speaking slot at the conference: 1. Prep AI prompt: use the Conference Research prompt + ask for talking points on local project challenges 2. Open with the science story — data made human 3. End with a specific call to action: “If your municipality has a water quality or habitat project that’s been stuck, come find us at the booth — or find me after this session.” 4. Collect cards from everyone who approaches you after

**A Note on Completing the Intake Form for Every Lead (Regardless of Qualification)**
Why do we complete the Municipal Champion Profile and start the Project Intake Form for every new Boil lead — even if we’re not sure they qualify yet?
Three reasons:
Qualification is confirmed by documentation, not impression. Conversations at events are fast and impressionistic. We often underqualify great leads and overqualify weak ones based on a 3-minute conversation. Completing the intake form forces a structured review that reveals the true picture — and sometimes surfaces a qualifying factor you missed in the initial conversation.
Speed matters when momentum is real. If a lead turns out to be highly qualified, having the intake form started saves days of back-and-forth. The discovery meeting (Step 3) runs much more effectively when you’ve already begun the profile.
The pipeline data has value beyond any single lead. Every intake form, whether qualified or not, builds your institutional knowledge about who is in the pipeline, what projects are stalled in the market, and where patterns are emerging. This intelligence informs strategy and grant applications.
Bottom line: the cost of starting an intake form is 10 minutes. The cost of not having one when a lead accelerates is weeks of catch-up.

text:
**STEP 3: CAPTURE & QUALIFY THE VISION**

**The Why — What This Step Accomplishes**
This is C-HAWQ’s Formal Intake Meeting — the structured discovery session where we evaluate whether there is a real, fundable project and a genuine champion behind it. The prospect has shown interest; now we apply rigor. We gather enough information to understand their project, their authority, their passion, and their alignment with what C-HAWQ can do. This is where we make the call: is this worth our full resources?
Before this meeting, an AI agent conducts deep background research on the municipality and the prospect. A prep summary and Plaud audio file brief are completed before anyone walks into this conversation. We do not wing this meeting. See the AI Pre-Meeting Research prompt below.

**Resources Deployed — Step 3**

**Before the Meeting — AI Research Package**
This step is non-negotiable. Before every formal intake meeting, the AI Agent runs the Municipality Research prompt to build a full prep brief. Meeting leads reviews and supplements with any additional context. This brief is completed 24 hours before the meeting and shared with all attendees.
What the prep package includes: 1. Municipality overview: geography, population, known water/habitat challenges 2. Champion profile: background, role, any public statements 3. Project intelligence: any prior studies, meeting minutes, or news coverage on the stalled project 4. Funding landscape: what grants or programs apply to this project type 5. Political landscape: commission composition, any known dynamics 6. Tailored discovery questions based on the research
AI Prompt — Pre-Meeting Research Package (run by AI Agent before every intake meeting):
I have a Formal Intake Meeting scheduled with [Name], [Title] at [Municipality, County, FL] on [Date].

Please build a complete pre-meeting research brief:

1. Municipality overview: population, coastal geography, any known water quality, stormwater, habitat, or canal issues. Any relevant CIP or master plan documents publicly available?
2. Champion profile: [Name]'s background, role history, any public statements on environmental topics, any prior involvement in relevant projects
3. Project intelligence: Any prior studies, commission meeting minutes, grant applications, or news coverage on [the specific project or issue, if known]
4. Funding landscape: What state and federal grants apply to this project type? Has the municipality received any relevant grants before?
5. Political landscape: Commission/council composition. Any environmental advocates or known skeptics?
6. Based on the above, draft 5 tailored discovery questions to ask this specific person
7. Draft a 2-sentence C-HAWQ intro customized for this audience

Please format this as a one-page briefing document I can review the morning of the meeting.

**The Formal Intake Meeting — Structure**
Format: 30–45 minute video or in-person meeting Attendees: You + ideally the Municipal Champion only (avoid committee-style first meetings) Tone: Curious, collaborative, expert. We ask more than we tell.
Meeting Agenda: 1. Opening (5 min): Thank them for their time. Brief C-HAWQ intro. “Tell me a little more about the project — I want to make sure we’re the right fit.” 2. Project Discovery (15 min): Ask the core qualifying questions below 3. C-HAWQ Value Alignment (10 min): Share how we’ve helped similar municipalities. Introduce the technical assistance grant concept. 4. Next Steps (5 min): If qualified, propose next meeting (Step 4).

**The C-HAWQ Discovery Deck**
Before the Formal Intake Meeting, the team prepares a custom, semi-custom discovery presentation to show the prospect. This deck introduces C-HAWQ, demonstrates our science-first approach, and uses visuals to open a conversation about what’s possible. It is not a pitch deck — it is a conversation starter.
The deck is prepared by Ryan Begin using a brief from Emily on what is known about the prospect and their community. AI assists in the visual research (satellite imagery, environmental data, comparable case visuals from the region). The champion sees their own geography and problem reflected back at them in a way that makes C-HAWQ feel like we’ve already been thinking about their specific situation.

**Qualifying Questions — Understanding Problem Areas**
Important framing: C-HAWQ does not go into the Formal Intake Meeting looking for a pre-existing project. We are looking for problem areas — environmental challenges that need solving. We help the municipality design the project. Ask these questions conversationally, not as a checklist.
Understanding Their Problem Areas: - What water or environmental issues keep coming up in your community that never seem to get resolved? - Where in your city does the environment feel most broken or neglected? - What do residents or local groups complain about most when it comes to your waterways, coastline, or canals? - If you had unlimited resources, what is the one environmental thing you’d fix in your municipality? - Are there areas where there have been repeated flooding, algae blooms, fish kills, habitat loss, or water quality violations?
Understanding Their Role and Motivation: - How did you come to be the person working on this? - What would it mean for you — professionally and personally — if this got solved? - Who else inside your organization cares about this? Who would push back?
Understanding the Landscape: - Have any consultants, engineers, or organizations looked at this before? What happened? - Is there any history of grant applications or environmental studies on this? - Where does this sit politically at the commission or council level? - What’s your timeline — is there any urgency, or is this a longer-term vision?
Understanding Fit: - Are you familiar with Public-Private Partnership (P3) funding structures? - Is the city in a position to be a partner in executing something, or is the expectation that someone else would own the execution?

**Qualifying Criteria — Is This a Boil-Priority Lead?**
A strong opportunity has ALL of the following:
The contact has real authority (city/county manager, department director, mayor, commissioner)
There is a specific, real project — not just a vague interest in “water quality”
The project has been stalled by a solvable problem (funding, engineering, political support) The Champion has personal passion, not just professional duty
The project aligns with C-HAWQ’s focus: coastal habitat, seagrass, water quality, canals
If most of these are present, this is worth investing in. Move to Step 4.

**P3 Candidacy Criteria — Is This a Strong P3 Candidate?**
Not every qualifying project is a strong P3 candidate. The following criteria indicate strong P3 potential. Use this to guide the funding strategy conversation:
Strong P3 indicators:
Project cost exceeds $500K — below this threshold, simpler procurement structures may be more appropriate
Multiple funding sources required — project needs a combination of grants, municipal contribution, and private capital
Long-term operational or maintenance component — P3 partners can take on long-term stewardship
Environmental outcomes can be monetized or credited — carbon credits, mitigation banking, water quality credits
There is a willing private or nonprofit capital partner — a P3 requires actual partners, not just intent
The municipality has procurement authority and political will — they can execute an RFP or cooperative procurement
Timeline allows for a 6–18 month procurement process — P3s take time to structure properly
Not a strong P3 candidate if: - Project is small and straightforward enough for standard grant + municipal contract - Municipality has no appetite for private partnership involvement - Project timeline is too compressed for a proper P3 structure - No viable private or capital partner exists for this project type
C-HAWQ can assist with the P3 structure even if the municipality has limited prior experience. Technical assistance grants are specifically designed to cover the cost of P3 planning, RFP drafting, and procurement support.

title: STEP 4: SCHEDULE THE NEXT STAGE
text:
**STEP 4: SCHEDULE THE NEXT STAGE**

**The Why — What This Step Accomplishes**
A Go decision means nothing if momentum dies in the days after. Step 4 is about locking in the next meeting and arriving with everything prepared to make that meeting decisive. Before the team shows up in the room, AI agents have already drafted a personalized briefing letter sent to the Champion, and Ryan has built a custom deck based on the problem areas and priorities the Champion described. The team reviews and approves everything before it goes out. This is C-HAWQ’s lean-team-with-AI-leverage model in action.

**What “Next Stage” Means**
The Step 4 meeting is usually one of:
A deeper problem-area conversation with the Champion + their team (department head, city manager, a commissioner)
A presentation to an internal group
A site visit to the location(s) of concern

**Resources Deployed — Step 4**

**How Step 4 Works — Agent-Assisted Preparation**
Before the meeting, two things are prepared by the team + AI:
1. A Personalized Briefing Letter to the Champion An AI agent drafts a letter to the Champion that:
Reflects back what they shared about their community’s problem areas
Explains how C-HAWQ can help address those specific challenges
Builds anticipation for the next meeting
Feels personal — not a form letter
Emily reviews and approves before it sends. This letter goes out within 48 hours of the Go decision.
AI Agent Prompt — Briefing Letter to Champion:
I just completed a Formal Intake Meeting with [Name], [Title] at [Municipality]. We made a Go decision. Here is everything I learned about their situation:

Problem areas they described: [summarize from intake notes]
Their personal motivation: [what drove them to this work]
Their community context: [what makes their municipality unique]
Blockers they mentioned: [funding, political, technical]
Their timeline expectations: [what they said]
People they mentioned bringing in next: [names/roles]

Please draft a personalized briefing letter from C-HAWQ that:
1. Opens by acknowledging what they shared — makes them feel truly heard
2. Connects their specific problem areas to what C-HAWQ does (not generic — specific to what they described)
3. Outlines the 2-3 ways C-HAWQ could realistically help based on what we know so far
4. Sets the frame for the next meeting: what we'll bring, who should be in the room, what we want to figure out together
5. Closes with genuine enthusiasm — not salesy

Voice: Warm, confident, science-first. C-HAWQ is their partner, not their vendor.
Length: 1 page maximum.
2. A Custom Presentation Deck Ryan (with AI research support) builds a tailored deck for the next meeting. The deck is built from what we learned in Step 3. It includes: - Their specific geography and environmental context (satellite/map imagery of the problem areas they mentioned) - Data relevant to their specific challenge (not generic Florida stats — localized data) - A visual of what’s possible: what restoration or improvement in their specific area could look like - A brief C-HAWQ overview framed around their problem, not our organization - A clear proposed path forward (not a contract — a conversation framework)
This deck is optional to present depending on how the meeting flows, but it’s always prepared and available.
AI Agent Prompt — Custom Deck Research Brief (for Ryan):
I need to build a custom presentation deck for a meeting with [Name] at [Municipality] on [Date].

Here is what I know from our intake meeting:
- Problem areas described: [list]
- Specific locations mentioned: [any water bodies, neighborhoods, areas]
- Their priorities and concerns: [list]
- Political context: [any commission dynamics]

Please prepare a research brief for our Creative Director that includes:
1. Satellite and map imagery sources for the specific locations they mentioned
2. Local environmental data relevant to their described problem areas (water quality readings, habitat loss data, flood history, etc.)
3. 2-3 comparable C-HAWQ-style project examples from Florida or the Southeast that would resonate for their situation
4. Key statistics or facts that quantify the problem in human terms for a general audience
5. Visual storytelling suggestions: what "before" looks like, what "after" could look like for this specific community

**Step 4 Presentation Framework — Consistent Slide Structure**
Every Step 4 custom deck is built on this 7-slide skeleton. Content in each slot is populated from the intake notes, AI research brief, and the Champion’s specific context. The framework ensures consistency across all projects regardless of who builds the deck.
Note on deck generation: The Step 4 deck is produced using deep AI research (AI Prompt — Custom Deck Research Brief above), then generated into a presentation using C-HAWQ’s standard production workflow. The framework below defines what must be in each slide; visual design follows C-HAWQ’s brand guide.
SLIDE 1 — COVER
SLIDE 2 — THE PROBLEM IN THEIR COMMUNITY
Required data (from intake form + AI research): Waterbody/habitat name · one localized environmental stat · how long the problem has persisted · community impact in plain terms
SLIDE 3 — WHAT’S POSSIBLE
Required data: 1–2 comparable Florida project examples with measurable outcomes (from AI research brief)

**STEP 5: FOSTER INTERNAL CURIOSITY**

**The Why — What This Step Accomplishes**
The Champion is sold. But the Champion can’t approve a project alone. Step 5 is about building grassroots momentum inside the municipality — so that when the project hits the commission or council agenda, it already has internal advocates across departments.
We use the same approach that worked on the Champion: science made emotional and real. Not a PowerPoint full of data. An experience that makes people feel what’s at stake and what’s possible.

**Resources Deployed — Step 5**

**Who We’re Reaching in Step 5**
Department staff who will implement the project
Adjacent departments who will be affected (public works, parks, finance)
City/county management staff
Internal communications or community outreach staff
Anyone who might become a blocker if they feel left out

**The Internal Engagement Approach**
Format options (choose based on what the Champion recommends):
1. Lunch-and-learn at the municipal facility (30-45 min presentation + Q&A)
2. Department meeting where C-HAWQ presents for 15-20 minutes
3. Informal walk-through of the C-HAWQ immersive display at their offices
The Frame: We are NOT selling. We are educating. We show up as a resource, not a vendor. The Champion introduces us.
The Agenda (for a lunch-and-learn or department meeting): 1. Champion introduces C-HAWQ: “I’ve been working with this team and I wanted you to hear directly from them about what’s possible.” 2. C-HAWQ opens with the science story: “Let me show you what this coastline looked like 30 years ago — and what’s possible if we move forward.” 3. Brief overview of the specific project: what it is, what it solves, what it would mean for the community 4. Q&A — welcome every question as legitimate 5. Close: “We’re not here to push anything. We’re here to be a resource. If this moves forward, our job is to make your team look like heroes.”

**SOP — Setting Up the Internal Engagement**
Ask the Champion: “Who else inside [municipality] needs to understand what we’re doing before this can move forward?”
Ask the Champion to make the introduction and host the meeting (they are the credibility bridge)
Coordinate logistics: date, location, who will attend, AV needs
Prepare customized materials: pull any local data, photos, or project parallels relevant to their specific community
Bring the immersive display if possible; if not, use the digital version

section: SECTION 6: PHASE 3 — MOBILIZATION (STEPS 7–8)
title: STEP 7: IMMERSIVE ENGAGEMENT
text:
**STEP 7: IMMERSIVE ENGAGEMENT**

**The Why — What This Step Accomplishes**
This is where C-HAWQ goes beyond conversation and lets the work speak for itself. The mobile science-museum experience is a transformational tool — it puts the public, the commission, students, and community leaders into direct sensory contact with the coastal habitat and water quality challenges facing their community. The goal: move the decision from the head to the gut. The Champion becomes a community hero in real time.

**C-HAWQ Resources Deployed — Step 7**

**What Is the Mobile Science-Museum Experience?**
A full immersive, interactive exhibit that travels to events, schools, parks, and public spaces in the municipality. It includes visual habitat displays, hands-on water quality demonstrations, scientific data panels, and storytelling designed for a general audience. It is not a trade booth — it is a genuine public education experience.
When to deploy:
City-sponsored community events
School visits (to build parent/voter awareness)
Waterfront festivals, parks, or nature centers
A formal community engagement event the Champion helps organize inside their city
Prior to a commission vote where public sentiment matters

**Community Outreach Partnership — How We Work With the Municipality**
C-HAWQ does not simply show up and run events on its own. We operate as a facilitator — the municipality is the sponsor, and the community’s trust in the municipality is what gives these events credibility. Before any event is planned:
Step 1 — Identify the Municipality’s Outreach Infrastructure Most municipalities have either a dedicated Community Outreach or Public Information Office, or they have established partner organizations (environmental nonprofits, neighborhood associations, civic groups) they have worked with before. Ask the Champion:
“Who handles public communications and community engagement for the city?”
“Are there organizations you’ve partnered with in the past for public education events?”
“Who in city government would need to be involved in approving a city-hosted event?”
Step 2 — Coordinate with the Municipality’s Outreach Team Schedule a planning meeting with the city’s outreach contacts before anything is finalized. The agenda for that meeting:
Brief them on what C-HAWQ’s mobile experience looks like and what it involves - Understand their existing event calendar and find dates that fit naturally (don’t create new events from scratch when possible)
Agree on roles: the municipality promotes, C-HAWQ delivers the educational programming
Confirm that key municipal staff will be present at events — this is not optional. The municipality’s visible participation signals to the community that this is a city-supported initiative, not an outside organization’s agenda.
Step 3 — Build a Volunteer Framework C-HAWQ cannot sustain a multi-event public engagement series alone. Events require:
C-HAWQ volunteers from our own organization for setup, staffing, and education delivery
Partner organization volunteers from local environmental groups, university clubs, or civic organizations with aligned missions
Municipal staff volunteers — department staff who can answer local questions and be visible community representatives
Academic team volunteers (as available) — grad students and advisors who can staff the science education component
Lorine coordinates the volunteer roster. Confirm volunteer headcount at least 2 weeks before each event.
Step 4 — Define the Event Structure Each public engagement event should have:
A clear co-host: C-HAWQ facilitates, the municipality/Champion hosts
An educational goal: what is the one takeaway we want every attendee to leave with?
A community feedback moment: sign-in sheet, comment cards, or brief survey
A call to action: how can an interested community member stay involved?

**SOP — Step 7: Deploying the Mobile Experience**
Coordinate with the Champion: Identify upcoming events in the municipality where the mobile experience makes sense. The Champion should invite C-HAWQ formally — this legitimizes your presence with the public.
Schedule and confirm logistics: Confirm dates, venue requirements (space, power, setup time), parking, and point of contact.
Pre-event community outreach (Champion’s team handles): Press release, social media posts, and local newsletter announcements that the Champion’s office pushes out — this is their win, not ours.
Set up the experience: Arrive 90 minutes early. Follow the standard setup SOP. Make sure Plaud Pin is active and recording the full event.
Work the room: Every team member is in relationship-building mode. Engage attendees with open questions, not pitches. Let the exhibit do the explaining. Capture names and contact info.
Capture the Champion’s moments: If the Mayor or Champion is present, make sure they are photographed and quoted — content for their own social media and press.
Post-event AI debrief: Immediately after the event, use your Plaud Pin recording to run the post-event AI debrief prompt.
Follow up within 48 hours: Send a follow-up email to every contact collected. Update GHL.

**Step 7 Qualifying Criteria — Is It Working?**
Community members are engaging with the exhibit (not just walking by)
The Champion is visibly proud to have C-HAWQ present in their community
Commission members or other decision-makers attended or are now aware
Local media coverage secured (even informal social media counts)
New community voices are now affiliated with the project — future political support

text:
**STEP 8: PROVIDE POLITICAL TAILWIND**

**The Why — What This Step Accomplishes**
By this stage, C-HAWQ has proven scientific credibility, engaged the community, and developed a project package. The final barrier to a formal funding commitment is almost never technical — it’s political. Step 8 is about building institutional confidence. We help the Champion navigate internal opposition, educate the commission on Public-Private Partnership structures, and ensure that when the vote comes, the “yes” is already in the room.

**C-HAWQ Resources Deployed — Step 8**

**What “Political Tailwind” Actually Means**
Commission members and city staff who were skeptical now understand the P3 model
The city attorney and finance director have had their questions answered
Community stakeholders (neighborhood associations, business groups, environmental orgs) are vocal advocates
There is no organized opposition — or if there is, we have a strategy for it
The Champion knows exactly what they’re walking into on vote day

**SOP — Step 8: Building Political Tailwind**
Map the political landscape with the Champion: Who on the commission is supportive? Who is skeptical? Who is silent? What are the specific concerns of each skeptical commissioner?
Commission Education Sessions: Offer to brief individual commission members 1-on-1 before any public vote. Keep it informal — coffee, a site visit, or a 20-minute briefing. This is where objections get neutralized privately before they become public drama.
P3 Education: Most municipal elected officials have never executed a P3 project. Demystify it. Provide a clear, plain-language explainer of how P3 structures work, what the city is responsible for, and how risk is shared.
Staff-Level Briefings: City manager, public works director, city attorney, finance director — these staff members often advise commissioners behind closed doors. Brief them too.
Community Voice Building: Help the Champion organize a petition, public comment letter-writing campaign, or coalition of community organizations that will show up to the commission meeting. The appearance of community support matters.
Media Strategy (Optional): If appropriate, help the Champion secure local media coverage before the vote — op-ed, news story, or interview. Earned media creates public momentum.
Pre-Vote Readiness Check: Confirm vote count with the Champion. If uncertain, delay the vote rather than risk a no.
Commission Meeting Support: Attend the vote. Be available for questions. Have leave-behinds ready.

**Key P3 Talking Points (Plain Language for Commissioners)**
What is a P3? A Public-Private Partnership is when a city partners with a private team to design, fund, build, and sometimes operate an infrastructure project. The city doesn’t pay the full cost upfront.
What does the city contribute? Typically the city provides land access, political will, and a portion of the funding — often through grants we help them secure.
Who handles the risk? Risk is shared and defined in the partnership agreement. C-HAWQ works only with vetted engineering and capital partners.
How is this different from just hiring a contractor? A contractor does what you tell them. A P3 partner brings their own capital, expertise, and accountability for outcomes.
What if a grant falls through? We structure projects with multiple funding pathways. No project is funded from a single source.

**Template 8A — Individual Commissioner Briefing Request (via Champion)**
Note: this email comes FROM the Champion, not from C-HAWQ directly. > Subject: Coffee this week? [Project Name] update > > Hi [Commissioner Name], > > I wanted to connect briefly before [Project Name] comes to a vote. I’ve been working with our partners at C-HAWQ on the project package, and I think a quick 20-minute conversation would be helpful — mostly so you can ask any questions before it’s on the public agenda. > > Would [Day/Time] or [Day/Time] work for a coffee or a quick call? > > [Champion’s Name]

**Template 8B — P3 Explainer Leave-Behind (1-Pager)**
WHAT IS A PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP (P3)? A plain-language guide for [City Name] commissioners and staff
The Basics A Public-Private Partnership (P3) is a funding and delivery model where a government entity (the City) partners with a private team to finance, build, and deliver a project. It’s used widely across the U.S. for infrastructure projects — roads, water systems, parks, and environmental restoration.
Why Consider a P3 for This Project? - The full project cost exceeds what the city wants to carry alone - Grant funding covers a portion, but not everything - A private partner brings capital, expertise, and delivery accountability - The city retains oversight and ownership of the outcome
How It Works (Simplified) 1. City agrees to project scope and partnership terms 2. Private partner (or consortium) provides a portion of capital 3. Grants (federal/state) cover another portion — C-HAWQ handles grant navigation 4. Project is executed by an agreed engineering/implementation team 5. City retains the asset; the environmental benefit belongs to the community
What the City Is NOT Doing - Not signing a blank check - Not transferring ownership of public land - Not giving up control of the project scope
Questions? Contact [Champion’s Name] or reach out to C-HAWQ directly.

**Political Socialization Workflow — Getting to a Council/Commission Vote**
Not every project requires a formal City Council or Commission vote to use a P3 structure — sometimes the project is simply incorporated into the Public Works project list and operating budget and it proceeds from there. Use this workflow to determine which path applies and how to navigate it.
STEP 1 — Determine If a Formal Vote Is Required
Ask the Champion: “Does your municipality require a formal commission or council vote to authorize a P3 engagement — or can Public Works proceed with this as part of the regular capital project list?”
STEP 2 — Build the Political Map (if vote required)
Before any outreach, ask the Champion to map the board:
“Who on the commission already knows about this project — and what do they think?”
“Who do you think will be the most supportive? Who might push back?”
“Is there anyone we should make sure is briefed before this ever hits an agenda?”
Output: A completed Stakeholder Map with disposition column filled in (Ally / Neutral / Skeptic / Blocker) for each council or commission member.
STEP 3 — Individual Council/Commission Member Briefings
Before any vote is scheduled, conduct one-on-one meetings with each council or commission member:
Who sets up the meetings: The Champion introduces C-HAWQ and requests the meeting on C-HAWQ’s behalf. C-HAWQ does not cold-contact elected officials.
Format: 15–30 minute meeting at their office, coffee, or over a brief call. Informal. No pressure.
What C-HAWQ brings: Politician-Friendly Presentation (AI prompt above), project visual package, P3 plain-language explainer, one-page leave-behind.
Goal: They leave informed and comfortable — not necessarily committed. Remove unknowns before the formal vote.
If a member declines a meeting: Note it on the Stakeholder Map. Brief the Champion and develop a secondary strategy (constituent letter, peer introduction, etc.).
Repeat until all members with a potential vote have been reached.
STEP 4 — Get the Project on the Agenda
Once the political groundwork is laid, the Champion works internally to place the project on the appropriate agenda:
Budget discussion or Capital Improvement Program (CIP) approval
P3 authorization vote
Project kickoff or engagement authorization
C-HAWQ’s role: Prepare all supporting documents for the public record. Coordinate with Champion on timing. Do not push for a vote before the political map is solid.
STEP 5 — If the Project Comes to Public Hearing or Formal Discussion
If the project is placed on a public agenda, C-HAWQ and the academic team attend:
What the academic team is prepared to explain: - What the science shows about this specific waterway or habitat - What the proposed project design would accomplish ecologically - Why this type of project delivers measurable, lasting community benefit - How similar projects have performed in comparable Florida municipalities
What C-HAWQ is prepared to explain: - The P3 structure and how it protects the municipality - The Exploration Grant and what the municipality is and is not committing to - C-HAWQ’s track record and organizational credibility
STEP 6 — The Vote
C-HAWQ and the Champion are both in the room.

**STEP 9: COMMIT TO FUNDING & PARTNERSHIP**

**The Why — What This Step Accomplishes**
This is the formalization step. The commission has (or is about to) vote yes. Now the legal, financial, and partnership scaffolding gets built. C-HAWQ’s job is to guide the Champion and the city through the P3 proposal process, confirm grant awards, execute partnership agreements, and ensure every party knows their role before a single shovel hits the ground.
This step is slow by design. Municipal procurement, legal review, and grant cycles take time. Your job is to stay organized, communicate proactively, and never let momentum die due to administrative delay.

**C-HAWQ Resources Deployed — Step 9**

**Key Deliverables in Step 9**

Grant award confirmations (or grant applications submitted and pending)
Project scope finalized and signed off by city

**Environmental Permitting — What to Expect**
Environmental permits are a non-negotiable component of most C-HAWQ projects. The permitting process is identified and structured during Step 9 as a formal requirement of the P3 agreement. Timelines vary significantly — plan for 6 months minimum, up to 2 years for complex projects.
Common permit pathways for C-HAWQ project types:
How permitting is handled in C-HAWQ projects:
During Step 9 agreement structuring, permitting requirements are identified and written into the P3 agreement as a project condition. The agreement specifies: - Which permits are required (based on engineering scoping from Step 6) - Who is the permit applicant (typically the municipality — they own the land) - Who prepares the applications (typically the Engineering Advisor or GC partner) - C-HAWQ’s role (coordination and regulatory liaison via legal counsel and technical advisors) - How permit timelines factor into the project schedule and funding agreement
C-HAWQ’s role in permitting:

**Jurisdiction Identification — Pre-Permit Site Review**
Status: This is C-HAWQ’s current draft process. Nathan Hewitt (GIS & Research Analyst, planned hire) will own this as a formal, repeatable task within the Project Execution Framework. Until then, the Program/Project Lead (Emily or Logan) initiates the intake and works in coordination with Zachary Lombardo’s firm to complete attorney consultation.
When to run this process: - Any project involving physical activity on or adjacent to a water body - Sites where land ownership or water body control is unknown or ambiguous - Prior to permitting conversations, MOU discussions, or landowner outreach - Not required for policy-only or advocacy-only scopes with no physical component
Purpose: Establish likely ownership of the water body and adjacent lands, flag regulatory obligations early, and ensure that attorney time with Zach is focused and efficient — not open-ended discovery.
STEP 1 — Site Intake
Complete the C-HAWQ Jurisdiction Identification Intake for the project site. Capture: - Water body type (canal, estuary, tidal creek, freshwater lake, etc.) - Tidal / navigable status (yes / no / unknown) - Known ownership signals (city-owned, county-owned, state sovereignty, private riparian, etc.) - Planned physical activity (water sampling, construction, shoreline modification, etc.) - Any prior research or studies on this site

STEP 2 — GIS Research

STEP 3 — Jurisdiction Briefing Memo
Produce a brief (1–2 page) jurisdiction memo from the intake and GIS research. The memo identifies: - Likely jurisdictional authority (municipal, county, state, federal, or combination) - Key regulatory flags (sovereign submerged lands, aquatic preserve, CCCL zone, WMD jurisdiction, etc.) - Priority research gaps (anything unresolved that Zach needs to answer) - Specific questions for legal counsel — do not schedule the attorney call without this list
File as: YYYY-MM_[Municipality]_[Project]_JurisdictionMemo.pdf in the project Google Drive folder.
STEP 4 — Attorney Consultation (Zach Lombardo)
Share the jurisdiction memo with Zachary Lombardo’s firm before any permitting conversations or MOU discussions. All attorney time is scoped and informed by Steps 1–3, which minimizes open-ended discovery billing.
Key questions Zach typically addresses: - Is the water body sovereign submerged land? Is a lease or consent of use required? - What is the appropriate permitting pathway (ERP, USACE Section 404, CCCL, etc.)? - Are there any title or ownership complications that need resolution before the project can proceed? - What is the likely regulatory timeline for this project type at this site?
STEP 5 — Site Record Update
Add jurisdiction findings to the project file and C-HAWQ’s internal site GIS layer. Flag any unresolved questions for ongoing monitoring.

(Step 4 — attorney consultation)
C-HAWQ does not submit permits on behalf of municipalities. We coordinate the process — connecting the right engineering and legal resources, identifying the required permits during scoping, and ensuring permit timelines are built into the project schedule and P3 agreement. C-HAWQ legal counsel (Zachary Lombardo) is the primary resource for sovereignty land lease questions and complex permit negotiations.
Sovereignty land lease note: Many C-HAWQ waterway projects involve state-owned submerged lands, triggering a sovereignty submerged lands lease or consent of use from the Florida DEP Board of Trustees. This is Zach’s primary regulatory specialty. Engage him at the start of Step 9 for any project involving direct work on tidal or navigable waterways. [AI prompt for sovereignty land lease assessment to be added — Emily to provide prompt from Zach’s guidance.]

**SOP — Step 9: Formalizing the Partnership**
Commission Vote: Attend the vote. Have a celebration ready for the Champion. Whatever the outcome, debrief immediately.
If the vote passes: Move to formal agreement drafting within 2 weeks. Strike while the iron is hot.
Engage legal teams: City attorney and C-HAWQ counsel review the P3 agreement. This takes time — set expectations up front with the Champion.
Confirm grant pipeline: Follow up on any pending applications. File any remaining applications. Confirm award letters.
Contractor and partner selection: C-HAWQ’s GC Intake Portal is the primary pipeline for qualified general contractors and environmental implementation partners. When a project reaches this stage, Lorine coordinates the opportunity posting through the portal. Registered GC partners can view posted projects and submit qualifications. subsection: What Is a P3 Under Florida Law?
title: What Is a P3 Under Florida Law?
text:
**What Is a P3 Under Florida Law?**
A Public-Private Partnership (P3) under Florida Statute § 255.065 allows municipalities to partner with private entities to deliver public projects using private capital, expertise, and efficiency. It is the legal framework that makes C-HAWQ’s model possible for coastal habitat and water quality projects.
Why P3 matters for C-HAWQ projects: - It allows a municipality to bring in private capital and expertise without traditional competitive bidding for every element - It creates a formal partnership structure that protects all parties - It enables the municipality to share risk with C-HAWQ and implementation partners - It is the primary vehicle for deploying private environmental investment alongside public grant funds

subsection: Step-by-Step: Guiding the Municipality Through P3 Procurement
title: Step-by-Step: Guiding the Municipality Through P3 Procurement
text:
**Step-by-Step: Guiding the Municipality Through P3 Procurement**
Step 1 — Commission Authorization The commission must pass a resolution authorizing staff to pursue a P3 procurement for the specific project. C-HAWQ legal counsel should assist in drafting the resolution language.
Step 2 — Qualifying Project Designation The project must be formally designated as a “qualifying project” under § 255.065. This is typically done by commission resolution or staff action depending on the municipality’s charter.
Step 3 — Procurement Method Selection The municipality’s procurement officer and city attorney decide on the procurement route (solicited RFP, unsolicited proposal, or hybrid). C-HAWQ recommends involving C-HAWQ legal counsel at this stage.
Step 4 — RFP Publication or Proposal Submission - If solicited: RFP is published with minimum 30-day response period (longer for complex projects) - If unsolicited: C-HAWQ or GC partner submits the proposal to the municipality’s procurement officer
Step 5 — Evaluation and Selection Municipality evaluates proposals using a published scoring criteria. C-HAWQ participates as technical advisor (not evaluator) unless C-HAWQ is a party to the P3.
Step 6 — Negotiation and Agreement Execution Final P3 agreement negotiated between municipality, GC partner, and C-HAWQ. C-HAWQ legal counsel manages this process in coordination with city attorney.
Step 7 — Commission Final Vote The executed P3 agreement is presented to the commission for final ratification. This is the formal “go” moment for construction-phase work.

title: WHY COMMISSION MEETINGS MATTER TO C-HAWQ
text:
**WHY COMMISSION MEETINGS MATTER TO C-HAWQ**
Municipal commission meetings are not just bureaucratic checkboxes. They are: - Intelligence gathering opportunities: You learn where the political winds are blowing, what other projects are competing for attention, and which commissioners are advocates vs. blockers. - Visibility moments: Your presence (even as an observer) signals commitment to the community and the Champion. - Vote days: These are the moments everything builds toward. - Relationship touchpoints: Before and after the meeting is some of the best networking you’ll do.
Rule #1: Never attend a commission meeting cold. You should always know what’s on the agenda, who the key players are, and what outcome you’re working toward.

section: SPECIAL MODULE A: CITY COUNCIL & COMMISSION MEETING PROTOCOL
title: PRE-MEETING PREPARATION
text:
**PRE-MEETING PREPARATION**

**1. Research the Agenda (Every Time)**
Commission agendas are public record. They are typically posted 3–7 days before the meeting on the city’s website.
Check for: - Is C-HAWQ’s project on the agenda? In what form? (Discussion item vs. action item vs. public comment period) - What else is on the agenda that might compete for commissioner attention or time? - Any items that could affect C-HAWQ’s project indirectly (budget discussions, other environmental projects, contractor controversies)?
AI Prompt — Agenda Research:
The [City Name] Commission meeting is on [Date]. The public agenda is available here: [URL or paste agenda text].

Our project, [Project Name], is [on/not on] the agenda. Our goal for this meeting is: [observe / present / support a vote / gather intelligence].

Please:
1. Summarize the full agenda in plain language — what decisions are being made?
2. Identify any items that could positively or negatively affect our project or the political climate around it
3. Are there any budget or procurement items I should understand before attending?
4. What intelligence should I be listening for during this meeting?
5. If I'm presenting today, what is likely to be top of mind for commissioners based on the rest of the agenda?

**2. Know Your Commissioners**
Before every meeting, refresh your knowledge of who will be in that room.
Know: - Full names and titles of all commissioners present - Their general stance on environmental/water quality issues - What ward/district they represent and what that community cares about - Any recent statements, votes, or local news involving them - Which ones have spoken positively about C-HAWQ’s project (your allies) and which ones are skeptical or unknown
Seating chart tip: Commission chambers are public spaces. Walk in early, find a seat with a sightline to the dais, and map who sits where. Names are often on placards.

**3. Prepare Your Materials**
Whether you’re presenting or just observing, bring: - [ ] 2-3 printed copies of the project one-pager (in case a commissioner or staff member asks) - [ ] Business cards - [ ] A notepad (or laptop/tablet for notes — know the room culture) - [ ] Your Plaud Pin, running and named correctly - [ ] A printed copy of the agenda with your notes

**4. Coordinate With the Champion in Advance**
Before any meeting where C-HAWQ’s project is involved: - Confirm what role you’re playing (observer vs. presenter vs. public comment) - Ask: “What do you need from me in the room?” - Confirm whether the Champion wants you to speak, stay quiet, or be available for questions - Agree on a signal system if needed (e.g., if they want you to speak up during public comment)

section: SPECIAL MODULE A: CITY COUNCIL & COMMISSION MEETING PROTOCOL
title: DURING THE MEETING — BEHAVIORAL PROTOCOL
text:
**DURING THE MEETING — BEHAVIORAL PROTOCOL**

**As an Observer**
Arrive 15–20 minutes early. Sign in if required. Introduce yourself to staff.
Take notes, not photos. Recording rules vary by municipality — check before you film anything.
Plaud Pin on. Set to record from the moment you arrive.
Read the room. Who is talking to whom before the meeting? Who looks engaged vs. checked out? Who arrives late or leaves early?
Stay until the end. Commissioners and staff are most accessible informally after the formal meeting ends.
Do not approach commissioners during the meeting. Wait until after or arrange a separate meeting.

**During Public Comment**
If you are making a public comment on behalf of the project: - Sign up on the speaker sheet when you arrive. - You typically have 2–3 minutes. Do not exceed your time. - Open with your name and organizational affiliation: “My name is [Name] and I represent C-HAWQ, Coastal Habitat and Water Quality Initiative.” - State your support for the project clearly and specifically. - Name the Champion if appropriate — “We are proud to be working alongside [Champion Name] on this initiative.” - Close with a specific ask: “We encourage the commission to [take action / authorize the next phase / support the budget allocation].” - Sit down. Do not argue, react to commissioner comments, or re-approach the podium unless invited.

**During a Formal Presentation**
If C-HAWQ is presenting to the commission: - Arrive 30–45 minutes early to test AV, confirm setup, and meet with staff. - Follow the timing guidelines you were given — err under, not over. - Address the commission as “Commissioner [Last Name]” unless they’ve indicated a preference. - Pause for questions naturally — do not barrel through. Commissioners want to feel heard. - If you don’t know the answer to a question: “That’s a great question — let me get you an exact answer in writing by [date].” Never guess. - After your presentation ends, take your seat and remain available for follow-up questions during discussion.

**After Public Business Closes**
The most valuable networking happens in the 30 minutes after the formal meeting: - Approach commissioners who were engaged or asked good questions. Thank them by name. - If a commissioner raised a concern, approach them: “Commissioner [Name], I heard your question about [X] — I’d love to get you more information on that. Would a brief call this week work?” - Introduce yourself to city staff members you haven’t met. - If the Champion is present, check in: “How do you feel it went? What’s next?”

**Working the Room**

Let them talk. Your job is to listen and qualify, not pitch.
Qualifying questions at events (from your Step 3 playbook): - “What kind of work does your city/organization focus on?” - “Are there any projects you’ve been trying to move forward that have hit a wall?” - “Who else in your city is working on water quality or coastal issues?” - “Have you ever worked with a P3 structure on an infrastructure project?”
When you find a qualified lead: - Get their card. - Ask permission to follow up: “Would it be okay if I reached out after the conference? I’d love to set up a brief call.” - Make a private note (in your phone or on the back of their card) about what you learned and what to reference in the follow-up.
When someone is not a fit: - Be gracious. They may be a referral source or future fit. - Add to Simmer (light nurture) in GHL. - Move on. Don’t spend 20 minutes with someone who can’t move the needle.

**Attending Sessions**
Sit near the front or in the aisle (easier to approach speakers after).
Take notes on relevant insights that you can reference in follow-up conversations.
Speakers are excellent prospects — they have credibility and often have municipal relationships. Introduce yourself immediately after their session.
Plaud Pin runs throughout all sessions you attend.

**Booth Operations (If Exhibiting)**
Booth goals: - Draw people in with genuine curiosity, not a hard sell - Qualify quickly, document contacts, move on to the next - Never let the booth be empty during open hours - Have a rotation so team members can attend sessions
Engagement approach at booth: > “Have you seen the seagrass data from [region]? We work with municipalities trying to turn that around — let me show you what we’ve been doing.”
Use the mobile science-museum experience as a conversation starter, not a closing tool.
Contact capture: Every meaningful conversation = a card, a sign-in, or a name in your notes. Do not rely on memory. The follow-up is where the value is.

**Evening Events and Social Time**
Conferences are often won in the evening. Dinners, receptions, and informal gatherings are where guards are down and real conversations happen. - Attend conference social events whenever possible. - Buy someone a drink before pitching anything. - If there is a speaker dinner or sponsor reception, prioritize it over everything else.

**SOP: Indoor Event Booth Setup**
1. Pre-Conference Coordination (1–2 weeks out) - Contact conference coordinator or hotel to confirm loading dock location, van parking, and service elevator access - Secure dedicated electricity for wave table and digital displays - Request corner booth or high-traffic corridor placement

4. Booth Assembly - Wave Table: position and lock wheels → anchor with four sandbags (one per wheel) → clamp pump hose to inner rim → fill from bin with zero spills → plug in wave maker - Booth: apply tablecloth → set backdrop → branded collateral in wooden bin → plug in monitor → set conference USB to loop - Island model on table if relevant for this audience
5. Tear-Down and Vehicle Security - Return empty water bin and island stand to van - Close rear doors → raise liftgate → fold manually into cradle → set holding pin → unplug remote - Remove wheel chocks → move van to designated parking

**SOP: Outdoor Event Booth Setup**
1. Pre-Event Coordination (1–2 weeks out) - Confirm booth site location and verify van can pull directly to site for unloading - Confirm power: battery generator charged and ready

3. 4. Outdoor Setup - Erect easy-up canopy first (shade and shelter) - Set up tables and chairs within canopy footprint - Position generator safely, plug in wave maker - Wave Table: lock wheels → four sandbags → fill from bin - Tablecloth → collateral in wooden bin → stickers displayed → island model on table if relevant → feather banners in stands
5. Tear-Down and Vehicle Security - Return empty water bin and unused stands to van - Close rear doors → fold liftgate into cradle → contact confirmed → holding pin set - Remove wheel chocks → move van to parking

section: SPECIAL MODULE C: CRM & GHL REFERENCE GUIDE
title: GHL OVERVIEW FOR C-HAWQ
text:
**GHL OVERVIEW FOR C-HAWQ**
Go High Level (GHL) is a comprehensive CRM and communication platform. C-HAWQ uses it to: - Track every contact in the outreach pipeline - Manage follow-up tasks and sequences - Send templated emails and sequences - Tag and segment contacts by pipeline stage and engagement level - Record notes from conversations, meetings, and events
The two primary lists: | List | Who Is In It | How You Treat Them | |——|————-|——————-| | Boil | Active outreach — municipalities, conservation nonprofits, and universities you are actively engaging | Regular, personalized outreach; active follow-up tasks; in the Proven Process sequence | | Simmer | Everyone else — past contacts, non-qualifying leads, referral connectors, contacts who aren’t ready yet | Light nurture — quarterly check-ins, newsletter/content updates, no hard outreach |
The rule: A contact graduates from Simmer to Boil when they have a qualified stalled project AND the relationship is warm enough to begin the Proven Process. A contact drops from Boil to Simmer if they disengage, are disqualified, or move to a wait-and-see hold.

What to log: - Every phone call or meeting (date, summary, outcome, next step) - Every email sent (note the template used and any personalization) - Every event interaction (conference name, what was discussed) - Any intelligence gathered about their city, project, or political landscape - Changes in their situation (new role, project status change, political shift)

GHL allows you to enroll contacts in automated email sequences. C-HAWQ uses these sparingly — only for Simmer contacts or for the initial cold outreach series at Step 1.

text:
**Simmer Contact Engagement Protocol — Mana Vision & Opt-In Rules**
The Legal Line: C-HAWQ cannot enroll contacts in any mass communication without explicit opt-in consent. This is a CAN-SPAM and Florida privacy law requirement. Contacts collected at events or added from research lists have not consented to marketing emails.
The Two-Track Simmer System:
How to collect opt-in consent:
At every conference, community event, or booth interaction: 1. Sign-in sheet — Include a checkbox: “✓ I’d like to receive occasional project updates and coastal science content from C-HAWQ.” Only checked contacts go on the Mana Vision list. 2. QR code — Links to a simple form with explicit opt-in. Post at booth and community events. Tag in GHL: Opted-In-Mana 3. Direct ask — After a good conversation: “Would it be okay if I added you to our occasional content updates? We share coastal science and project progress — nothing frequent.”
Mana Vision: [PLACEHOLDER — Ryan Begin’s team and community engagement platform. Full distribution protocol to be added when v1 is shared with Emily. GHL tag for opted-in contacts: Opted-In-Mana]
Non-opted-in Simmer contacts: Quarterly individual outreach only. Reference something specific — a project update in their region, a relevant news story, a conference you know they attend. No templates. No sequences.

section: SPECIAL MODULE F: PROJECT VIDEO & PHOTO DOCUMENTATION GUIDE
title: The Vision — Why Documentation Matters
text:
**The Vision — Why Documentation Matters**
Every C-HAWQ project is a story of community transformation. The photo and video documentation that happens throughout the project lifecycle has three audiences: 1. The municipality and its community — proof that their investment and trust produced something real 2. Future Champions — the case study content that makes Steps 1–4 faster for the next municipality 3. National media and conference audiences — the proof points that establish C-HAWQ as a national leader in science-driven coastal restoration
This is not an afterthought. Documentation is a core deliverable at every phase from Step 7 forward.

section: SPECIAL MODULE F: PROJECT VIDEO & PHOTO DOCUMENTATION GUIDE
title: Phase-by-Phase Video & Photo Arc
text:
**Phase-by-Phase Video & Photo Arc**

**Phase 1 — The Weight of the Problem (Steps 7–8: During community mobilization)**
Goal: Establish the emotional hook. Capture the “before” — the current state of the waterbody and what it means to the community.
The Community Member (The Stakeholder): - Interview question: “What did this [lake/waterway/habitat] used to mean to families here, and what has it been like watching it decline over the last 10 years?” - Visuals: B-roll of them looking at the site, holding an old photo of what it used to look like
The Municipal Champion (The Hero): - Interview question: “Before C-HAWQ, what were the 3:00 AM worries? What was the one hurdle that felt like a brick wall?” - Visuals: Close-up shots in their office; outdated maps or permit stacks in the background

**Phase 2 — Clearing the Fog (Step 8–9: During political alignment and partnership formation)**
Goal: Show C-HAWQ as the “Expert Guide” that simplifies the complex.
The Municipal Champion (The Pivot): - Interview question: “Once C-HAWQ stepped in, what was the first lightbulb moment where you realized this project was actually going to happen?” - Interview question: “How did having a dedicated team of experts change your daily workload on this project?” - Visuals: Blueprint motion graphics overlaying digital designs over the real site; the Visionary Narrator explains how C-HAWQ translated bureaucracy into a plan

**Phase 3 — The Transformation (Steps 9–10: During construction)**
Goal: Document the grind and the progress.
The Grad Student or On-Site Researcher (In-the-Field): - Visuals: GoPro POV shots — water sampling, site inspections, talking to contractors - Narrator: The 1–2 year construction timeline told through construction milestone infographics (use brand green #3f886c)

**Phase 4 — The Proof (Step 10: At completion)**
Goal: Validate success through data and human relief.
The Grad Student / Academic Advisor (The Expert): - Interview question: “Based on the data we’ve been monitoring for [X] months, what tangible results are we seeing in water quality / habitat / biodiversity?” - Interview question: “As a researcher, what does it feel like to see your science turn into a physical solution for this town?”
The Municipal Champion (The Hero’s Reward): - Interview question: “Now that the dust has settled, what does this project mean for the future of your municipality?”
The Community Member (Full Circle): - Visuals: Them using the restored space — fishing, walking, kayaking, watching their kids play near water

section: SPECIAL MODULE F: PROJECT VIDEO & PHOTO DOCUMENTATION GUIDE
title: The Grad Student Field Guide
text:
**The Grad Student Field Guide**
The academic researcher on site for the 1–2 year project period is C-HAWQ’s most valuable documentation asset. Give them this checklist from day one:
Fixed-Point Time-lapse: Identify one specific spot on site. Every visit, record a 10-second video from that exact angle, same time of day. Over 18 months this becomes the most powerful content we have.
POV Action Shots: Use a GoPro (chest mount) for technical inspection moments — looking at water samples, pointing at specific site features, walking the construction zone.
Daily Discovery Audio Memo: Record a quick voice memo whenever they hit a milestone or solve a problem. Used as “scratch VO” to guide the professional narrator in post.
Drone Footage: If they hold a FAA Part 107 certificate, explore purchasing a DJI Mini for periodic aerial progress documentation. Coordinate with Ryan Begin before purchasing.

**SPECIAL MODULE E: FUNDING NAVIGATION & PROCUREMENT OPTIONS**
Purpose: C-HAWQ’s role is not just to identify funding — it is to help municipalities navigate the entire funding and procurement process so they can actually execute. This module explains C-HAWQ’s approach to helping a municipality define and structure their funding plan.

section: SPECIAL MODULE E: FUNDING NAVIGATION & PROCUREMENT OPTIONS
subsection: What C-HAWQ Offers in Funding Navigation
title: What C-HAWQ Offers in Funding Navigation
text:
**What C-HAWQ Offers in Funding Navigation**
When a municipality qualifies and a Go decision is made, C-HAWQ becomes the municipality’s active partner in defining the funding plan. This is one of the most valuable things we do — and it is not something most municipalities can navigate on their own.
Our funding navigation services include: 1. Grant identification and application — we identify the most applicable federal and state grants, match them to project specifics, and coordinate the application process 2. P3 structure design — we help the municipality understand, evaluate, and structure a Public-Private Partnership appropriate for their project 3. Technical assistance grants — C-HAWQ can provide up to $200,000 in technical assistance grants to fund the cost of procurement planning, RFP development, P3 structuring, and grant writing 4. Contractor identification — we help the municipality identify contractors who specialize in finding and securing matching funds for P3 projects 5. Procurement document preparation — we support the development of RFP and procurement documents so the city can execute a proper competitive process

section: SPECIAL MODULE E: FUNDING NAVIGATION & PROCUREMENT OPTIONS
subsection: Exploration Grant Partnership Agreement — Legal Framework
title: Exploration Grant Partnership Agreement — Legal Framework
text:
**Exploration Grant Partnership Agreement — Legal Framework**
What this section covers: The formal legal documents governing C-HAWQ’s technical assistance engagement with a qualifying municipality — including how the Exploration Grant (up to $200,000 in fee-free services) is structured, what the municipality agrees to, and how the partnership is protected for both parties.
The structure (overview): 1. The municipality submits a grant interest form via the C-HAWQ website, which generates an automated confirmation receipt — this is the start of the formal record. 2. After a Go or Conditional Go decision, C-HAWQ issues a Municipal Partnership Agreement covering: - Scope of technical assistance services C-HAWQ will provide - Municipality’s commitments (staff time, site access, cooperation with advisors) - Grant allocation amount authorized - IP and data ownership (all deliverables remain the municipality’s property) - Exit/withdrawal terms for either party 3. As the project advances toward execution (Step 9), a P3 Partnership Agreement is executed between the municipality, C-HAWQ, and the implementation partner — this is the binding agreement for the funded project.

**Technical Assistance Grants — What They Cover**
C-HAWQ’s technical assistance grants are specifically designed to fund the cost of getting to execution — not the project itself. They cover:
Grant writing services for applicable state and federal programs
P3 feasibility analysis and structure design
RFP drafting and procurement document preparation
Engineering scoping and preliminary cost estimation
Environmental assessment coordination
Community engagement and public process support
Legal review coordination (city attorney support for P3 agreement review)
Contractor vetting and matching funds identification
Up to $200,000 is available in technical assistance when there is full alignment between the project and C-HAWQ’s mission. Technical assistance grants are contingent on: 1. A completed Go/No-Go assessment with a Go or Conditional Go outcome 2. A completed Project Intake Form and Municipal Champion Profile 3. C-HAWQ board authorization

title: Finding a Contractor for Matching Funds
text:
**Finding a Contractor for Matching Funds**
One of the most underutilized funding strategies for Florida municipalities is finding a contractor or P3 partner who takes responsibility for identifying and securing matching funds. C-HAWQ facilitates this through:
Our partner network — C-HAWQ maintains relationships with environmental engineering firms, conservation-focused developers, and environmental investment groups who have experience in P3 coastal and water quality projects in Florida
P3 contractor RFQ process — for qualifying projects, we help the city issue a Request for Qualifications to identify P3-capable partners who can bring capital
Matching fund research — The AI Agent runs research to identify other funding sources (RESTORE Act, NOAA, EPA 319, SFWMD cost-share programs) that could serve as matching funds for a primary grant

**C-HAWQ Grant Intelligence Application**
C-HAWQ’s Grant Intelligence App — built and maintained by Ryan Begin — is the live, primary reference for grant program research. The app scrapes and catalogs historical and upcoming grant programs relevant to Florida coastal restoration, including FDEP, SFWMD, RESTORE Act, NOAA, EPA 319, and others, with eligibility requirements, typical award ranges, and application windows updated continuously.
Use the Grant Intelligence App for: - Step 6: Identifying applicable programs for a specific project type - Step 9: Confirming application windows and current program status - Any time a Champion asks “is there a grant for this?”

**Blue Green Accelerator — Operational Terms**
Every project that passes a Go decision operates under C-HAWQ’s Blue Green Accelerator program. These terms govern how the technical assistance is delivered and what it covers. The team must understand these clearly — both for internal budget management and for explaining the program to Champions.
Form of Award: Direct technical services — not cash disbursement. C-HAWQ manages all third-party vendor payments, expert honorariums, and student stipends directly. No funds are transferred to the municipality. The municipality receives the outputs (research reports, engineering visuals, grant applications) — not a check.

**Why This Is Core to the Model**
Most of what stalls a municipal environmental project is the absence of credible, project-specific primary data. A city cannot apply for a $1M FDEP grant without a scientific baseline. They cannot present to their commission without defensible environmental data. Graduate students — under the supervision of tenured professors at UF, USF, and UF|IFAS — produce this data at a fraction of the cost of a private consulting firm, while generating publishable research that elevates C-HAWQ’s academic credibility.
Current university partnership status: - Verbal commitments in place with academic advisors at UF and USF - Formal MOU with University of Florida in development — pending project examples for Dean review - Student compensation: funded through C-HAWQ’s Blue Green Accelerator (C-HAWQ funds), expected to flow to the professor’s department to cover student tuition and stipend — exact mechanism to be confirmed with professors (see question list at end of this module)
